rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all six peaks and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The elution window will guide subsequent slope and temperature tests.
Injection 1 already attained the maximum CRF of 1.000. Shorten the gradient by one grid step to test whether that score can be maintained with faster elution, keeping the other parameters fixed.

The shorter gradient retains maximum CRF, but the critical pair is now close to the resolution threshold. Raise temperature while holding the gradient fixed to test whether temperature improves its selectivity and further shortens elution.

At 50 C every pair remains fully resolved, with improved resolution of the central critical pair. Shorten the gradient another step to test the fastest fully resolved method while retaining the established maximum-score methods as fallbacks.

Reduce the gradient slope by lowering phi1, which should restore resolution of the central pair while remaining faster than injection 3. The last peak previously eluted near 0.53 organic fraction, so 0.80 leaves ample elution strength.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to reduce early waiting time while making the gradient slightly shallower. This tests whether the maximum CRF can be retained with faster final elution; the first peak previously eluted near 0.21 organic fraction.

Increase phi0 one more grid step to shorten elution while slightly reducing gradient steepness. Injection 6 improved the critical-pair resolution, and its first peak remains sufficiently retained to justify this test.

Continue increasing phi0 by one grid step to seek faster elution at the maximum CRF. Monitor the first pair for loss of retention and the central pair for selectivity changes as the starting composition approaches the early elution window.

Test one further increase in starting organic fraction to shorten the run while preserving full resolution. The early peaks are approaching the unretained region, so their separation may now limit further increases in phi0.

Slightly flatten the gradient to recover the central pair, which narrowly missed full resolution at R = 1.46. This should retain much of injection 9's speed advantage, with ample final organic strength to elute the last compound.

Maximum CRF is already secured, so test a much steeper gradient for a faster, potentially reordered separation. The central pair may separate again after an elution-order crossover; this injection tests that possibility directly.

Test whether lower temperature improves selectivity on the steep-gradient branch, where the central pair may have reversed order. Lowering phi0 should also protect early-pair retention; established maximum-CRF methods remain available if this fast separation fails.

Return near the fully resolved conditions of injection 8, increasing slope modestly from 0.100 to 0.1125 organic fraction per minute to shorten elution. The final fraction remains above the observed late-peak elution window, while the central pair should be near the resolution threshold.

Raise temperature one step to test whether the central pair's small resolution deficit can be recovered while shortening elution. Earlier temperature tests improved central-pair selectivity but compressed the first pair, so both pairs will determine success.
Use a slope between injections 9 and 10 to target full central-pair resolution with a last peak earlier than injection 10. Returning to 50 C protects the early pair, which lost resolution at 55 C.

Test a higher starting fraction at lower temperature, keeping injection 15's gradient slope. Lower temperature may preserve early-peak retention while the changed starting composition explores a different central-pair selectivity regime.

Test whether combining a higher starting fraction with a steep gradient can separate the central pair on the opposite side of its selectivity crossover. Use 25 C to support early-peak retention; injection 15 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Test whether a higher starting fraction strengthens separation of the central pair on the fast-gradient branch while the shallower slope improves the late pair. This is an exploratory speed test with a risk of compressing the early peaks; maximum CRF is already secured.

Return to the established fully resolved region and test a slope between injections 8 and 13. This should recover the central pair above R = 1.5 while shortening elution relative to injection 8, without pushing the first peak into the unretained region.

Test whether a shallower gradient can restore central-pair resolution at phi0 = 0.30, with a modest temperature increase relative to injection 16. This explores a narrower operating window while retaining injection 15 as the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Test a compact gradient near the successful region, lowering phi0 to give the early peaks more retention. This should offer better resolution margins than injection 15 while maintaining maximum CRF and a short elution time.

Flatten the gradient modestly relative to injection 15 to strengthen its marginal central-pair resolution while retaining the faster starting composition. This targets a more forgiving maximum-CRF method, with only a small expected increase in elution time.

Trim injection 8's gradient endpoint and duration while preserving its successful slope and temperature. All six peaks should elute before the gradient ends, retaining maximum CRF with a shorter programmed gradient.

Lower the endpoint one step to improve the central-pair resolution margin of injection 23 while keeping the early peaks retained. The last peak previously eluted near 0.50 organic fraction, so this endpoint should still support complete elution well within 10 minutes.

Use the final injection to test temperature sensitivity around injection 24, whose minimum resolution was 2.33. A 5 C reduction should preserve maximum CRF with ample time margin and establish whether this compact method tolerates a temperature change.
